items.prompt: Define a directed response, and state what it is not.
items.canonical_answer: A directed response is a new text written from a source for a form, audience and purpose the task sets, re-using the source’s content in a new style. It is not a summary of the source and not a copy of its wording: the content is carried across, and everything else — register, voice, structure — is built for the new reader the task names.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: a new text from a source, for a set form, audience and purpose, re-using its content.
The boundaries — not a summary, not a copy — are part of the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: State the two steps of reshaping a source.
items.canonical_answer: First select: from everything the source contains, keep the content the new purpose needs and leave the rest. Then change: register, voice and structure go over to the new form, and the content arrives in your own words. The order matters, because selecting first means every sentence is written for the new reader rather than translated from the old one.
marking_guidance: Credit the two steps in order: select, then change.
The order is the point: an answer that translates sentence by sentence has reversed it.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between re-using a source’s content and lifting its wording, and what is the test?
items.canonical_answer: Re-using content keeps what the source says — facts, viewpoint, people — in your own words; lifting copies phrases or sentences across, which is copying rather than re-use. The test is the sentence’s authorship: could the source’s writer have written it? If yes, it is theirs, and the response has changed clothing without changing voice — the one thing reshaping must do.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: content carried in new words against wording copied across.
Must give the test: whether the source’s writer could have written the sentence.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: This extract is from a source about a library campaign: "The council announced on Tuesday that the library will remain open, with reduced hours, after a petition gathered 4,000 signatures. Volunteers will staff the weekend counter." Rewrite it as the opening of an email to a friend who signed the petition, keeping the content.
items.canonical_answer: Guess what — it worked! The council said on Tuesday the library stays open, though the hours are cut, and that was after all those signatures (4,000 of them — including yours). The weekends will be run by volunteers, so no more Saturday staff, but the doors stay open. I know you signed, so this one is partly yours. (Any rewrite keeps the three facts — the announcement, the reduced hours, the petition’s size and the volunteers — inside an email’s conventions, in an informal register the friend has earned.)
marking_guidance: Credit the rewrite: the extract’s content carried across, because the words show the re-use.
Credit the fit to the form: an email’s greeting and register, so the change of style shows in the words.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: This extract is from a source about a library campaign: "The council announced on Tuesday that the library will remain open, with reduced hours, after a petition gathered 4,000 signatures. Volunteers will staff the weekend counter." Rewrite it as the opening of a formal public notice, keeping the content.
items.canonical_answer: PUBLIC NOTICE — LIBRARY SERVICE UPDATE. Following Tuesday’s council decision, the library will remain open under revised operating hours. The decision follows a petition of 4,000 signatures. Weekend counter services will in future be staffed by volunteers. Full hours are displayed at the entrance. (The rewrite keeps the three facts and gives them the notice’s register: impersonal, nominalised, and addressed to the public as a body.)
marking_guidance: Credit the rewrite: the extract’s content carried across into the notice’s words.
Credit the register change: impersonal and formal, because the words show the notice doing its public work.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A directed response begins: "The article tells us that the scheme, ‘a beacon of community spirit’, has ‘transformed the lives of thousands’." What is the learner doing, and what is the cure?
items.canonical_answer: The error is lifting: two of the source’s phrases travel into the response inside quotation marks, which is copying rather than re-use — the words show the source’s voice, not the new text’s. The cure is to write every sentence afresh for the new reader: the beacon of community spirit becomes, for the new audience, whatever the new voice would actually call it — "the whole street turned up", for a friend; "strong local participation", for an official — so the content crosses and the wording does not.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: the source’s phrases copied into the response.
Must give the cure: each sentence written afresh for the new reader, because the words show whose voice is speaking.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner’s directed response retells the source from start to finish in the source’s order, at half its length. What has gone wrong, and what does the task actually ask for?
items.canonical_answer: The error is summarising: retelling the source in its own order produces a shorter source, not a new text, because selection and reshaping never happened. The task asks for a new form for a named audience and purpose — which means choosing the content that purpose needs (and dropping the rest), then rebuilding it in the register and structure of the new form. A summary keeps everything in its place; a response keeps the right things in new places.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: a summary in the source’s order instead of a reshaped text.
Must state what the task asks for: selection for the new purpose, and rebuilding for the new form and audience.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A response to a source about a rescued swimmer adds a detail the source never mentions: that the swimmer had ignored warning signs earlier that day. Why does the addition matter, and what is the rule?
items.canonical_answer: The addition matters because it drifts the response into a different story: the source’s rescue becomes a tale about recklessness, and the new fact carries a judgement the source never made. The rule is that every fact in a directed response traces back to the source — the response re-uses what is there, and invents nothing, because the reader’s trust in the whole answer rests on the two texts telling one story.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: the addition changes the story the source tells.
Must give the rule: every fact in the response traces back to the source, so nothing is invented.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What does writing in the style of a text mean?
items.canonical_answer: It means taking on the text’s register, its sentence patterns, its voice and its signature features, so a continuation reads as if the same writer wrote it. The style is not one of these things alone: a continuation with the right words in the wrong sentence shapes sounds like someone doing an impression, which is why the four are held together.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: register, sentence patterns, voice and signature features, all taken on.
An answer about copying the topic has confused style with content.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Give the steps for matching a text’s style.
items.canonical_answer: First name its register: formal, conversational, urgent? Then its typical sentence: long and subordinated, or short and clipped? Then its voice: ironic, confiding, measured? Then two signature features: the aside in dashes, the rule-of-three close, the direct address. Then write with all of them held in mind at once — the continuation is judged by how many of the four it carries, and by how few of its own habits it lets in.
marking_guidance: Credit the steps in order: register, typical sentence, voice, two signature features, then write.
The last step — writing with them held together — is the one that makes the rest worth doing.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Here is an extract, written for the purpose: "The instructions for assembling this desk are, I can now report, a work of fiction. The diagram shows a calm person with two hands. I have four hands’ worth of questions." Continue it for two sentences in the same style.
items.canonical_answer: A continuation in the same style would run: "Step four, for instance, mentions a dowel that appears nowhere in the parts list, and step five mentions it twice. I have written to the manufacturer, in the manner of a person who no longer expects to sleep tonight." (Any two sentences that keep the register, the first-person exasperated voice, the long sentence with a dry aside, and one signature feature such as the deadpan arithmetic are a match.)
marking_guidance: Credit the continuation: two sentences in the extract’s text, because the fit is the skill tested.
Credit the style held in the words: the dry aside, the first person, the register — so the continuation shows the match.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: List the five things decoded from a directed-response task before writing.
items.canonical_answer: The role: who am I? The form: what kind of text? The audience: who reads it? The purpose: what must it do? And the source content: which facts and viewpoints must come across? Five answers, written down, and every sentence of the response is then checked against them.
marking_guidance: Credit the five in order: role, form, audience, purpose, source content.
The sequence is a decode, so an answer with four of the five has a response built on a missing premise.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Why does the role a task sets matter so much to the writing?
items.canonical_answer: The reason is that the role decides the voice and the point of view, and both are in every sentence: a head learner writes with authority and accountability, a visitor with curiosity and gratitude, and a shopkeeper with the detail of the counter. Writing as the role means staying inside that voice — its knowledge, its stakes, its loyalties — which is why writing about the role, as a reporter would, produces sentences no actual head learner would say.
marking_guidance: Credit the reason: the role fixes the voice and point of view of every sentence.
An answer that says roles matter because the task says so has not explained the why.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between writing as a role and writing about it, and how does the difference show in the sentences?
items.canonical_answer: Writing as the role stays inside its voice: "I have watched this town change for thirty years" is a resident speaking. Writing about the role steps outside: "The residents of the town have watched it change" is a reporter describing. The difference shows in the pronouns, in what the sentence can know (an insider’s memory against a survey’s fact), and in the address — the insider can say "we", the outsider cannot, and the task’s role decides which sentence is available.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: inside the voice against outside it.
Must say how it shows: pronouns, what the sentence can know, the address — so the difference is visible in the words.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What does a 150–200-word directed response contain, and how are the words shared?
items.canonical_answer: It contains the form’s key conventions, the source’s relevant content and a register fitted to the reader. The words are shared across an opening that establishes the form and voice, a body that carries the content in two or three developed moves, and a close that lands the purpose — roughly forty, a hundred and forty, twenty. The range is part of the task: the task sets 150–200 words from an unseen source of about 550–750, and the response’s fit to its length is part of its fit to the form.
marking_guidance: Credit the features: form’s conventions, relevant content, fitted register — the response contains all three.
Credit the sharing: opening, body, close, because the words are budgeted, not poured.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Give a plan for sharing 150–200 words across a directed response.
items.canonical_answer: First, the opening: about thirty to forty words, establishing the form’s convention and the role’s voice. Then the body: about a hundred to a hundred and twenty, carrying the source’s content in two or three developed moves — each one a fact plus its meaning for the new reader. Then the close: about twenty, landing the purpose — the ask, the verdict, the sign-off. Three sections, budgeted before writing, so the length is used rather than reached.
marking_guidance: Credit the three sections with their word shares, in the order: opening, body, close.
The budget is a plan, so an answer that says "write and see" has not planned.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A task sets a speech to a school assembly from a source about a sponsored walk. Opening A: "This walk raised a lot of money which will help the school and the charity, and I would like to tell you about it." Opening B: "Good morning, assembly. Eleven kilometres. Thirty-one of you. One very proud teacher. Let me tell you what Saturday did." Which better fits the form and audience, and what is the case against the other?
items.canonical_answer: B fits better: it carries the speech’s convention (a greeting to the hall), the tricolon of figures, and the speaker’s evident role and pride, and the short sentences suit a listening audience that must be caught at once. The case against A is that it neither addresses the hall nor carries a voice — it could open a report as easily as a speech, so the form is unannounced and the audience unmet. However, A does state its purpose plainly, which is its one virtue; B does that too, in its last sentence.
marking_guidance: Credit the judgement: B, with the reasons drawn from the speech’s features and their effect on the hall.
Credit the case against A with its evidence: no address, no voice, a form that could be anything — however, note its plain purpose if the answer sees it.
The strongest answers name the test: A could open any text; B could only open a speech.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner’s 200-word speech never addresses the hall and never signposts where it is going. What convention damage has been done, and why does it cost the task marks?
items.canonical_answer: The error is leaving out the form’s conventions: a speech with no address to its audience and no signposting has not shown its form, and the reader must guess it from the content — which the task asked the writer to demonstrate. The convention damage costs the writing marks because the fit to form is part of the fit to the task: the greeting finds the hall, the signposting keeps the listeners, and a speech that does neither is an essay read aloud.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: the speech’s conventions, address and signposting, left out.
Must say why it costs marks: the form is part of the task, so a reader forced to guess the form is reading a poorer fit.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner writes 320 words for a task set at 150–200, "because there was so much good material in the source". Why does the extra material not help, and what is the judgement on length?
items.canonical_answer: The extra material does not help because the range is part of the task: an answer well outside 150–200 words is a poorer fit to the form and purpose, whatever the quality of what it carries — the task asked for selection as well as reshaping, and 320 words shows the selection never happened. The judgement on length is fit, not a penalty per word: no fixed sum is deducted, but a response that has sprawled past its form (or withered under it) has missed one of the task’s own requirements.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: writing far outside the range, when the range is part of the task and selection was being tested.
Must state the judgement: length is judged as fit to form and purpose, not as a word-by-word penalty.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define the comparison task, and state its marks.
items.canonical_answer: The comparison sets your own directed response beside the source, opens with the instruction Compare, and analyses form, structure and language across both. It is worth fifteen marks — five for the comparative reading of both texts, ten for the analysis — and the analysis explains the similarities and differences by each text’s purpose, audience and context.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the source and your own response compared, on form, structure and language.
The marks — fifteen, split five for reading and ten for analysis — are part of the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Give the steps for planning a comparison of two texts.
items.canonical_answer: First, fix each text’s purpose, audience and form — the frame every feature is judged against. Then list the features each text carries. Then match them in pairs: the source’s opening beside the response’s, its voice beside the response’s, its sentence shapes beside the response’s. Then plan the paragraphs on the pairs, one pair per point, so both texts are in every paragraph before a sentence is written.
marking_guidance: Credit the steps in order: frames, features, pairs, paragraphs.
The pairing is the step that makes it a comparison, so an answer without it has planned two descriptions.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Name five comparative connectives and say what each does.
items.canonical_answer: Whereas marks a difference; similarly marks a likeness; in contrast marks a sharper difference than whereas; both holds the two texts in one subject; unlike marks what one has and the other lacks. Each connective is the visible machinery of a paired point, which is why a paragraph of comparison carries at least one, and a paragraph of description carries none.
marking_guidance: Credit the five: whereas, similarly, in contrast, both, unlike, with what each does.
The features are named as machinery, so an answer that lists them without their jobs has half the card.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Pair A opens: "The forgotten hero of Keetmanshoop is a man nobody remembers." Pair B opens: "Dear Ms Angula, I am writing with real concern about the crossing on our street." Write one comparative sentence about these openings.
items.canonical_answer: Whereas Pair A opens with a paradox that teases its reader into the article — "a man nobody remembers", an invitation to find out — Pair B opens with a salutation and a stated purpose, because a letter must find its reader before it can state its case, while an article must first be chosen. (Any sentence that holds both openings in one grammar, on a connective, and explains the difference by purpose or audience meets the task.)
marking_guidance: Credit the sentence: both openings held in one sentence, because the pairing is the skill.
Credit the explanation by purpose or audience, so the comparison carries a reason, not just an observation.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A comparison gives the source nine paragraphs and the response two, in passing. What has gone wrong, and what is the habit that fixes it?
items.canonical_answer: The error is writing mostly about the source and little about the response, which abandons half the subject and half the marks — the task exists because there are two texts. The fixing habit is the paired point: no paragraph stays on one text longer than a sentence before referring across, and each point is built on a connective from the first word. The check is arithmetic: count the sentences naming each text, and the counts should be close.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: one text treated as the subject and the other as a footnote.
Must give the habit: the paired point in every paragraph, with a connective, and the countable balance it produces.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Both texts are about the dam project and both mention the cost." Why is this not comparison of the kind the task rewards, and what is the missing half?
items.canonical_answer: The learner has compared what the texts say, and the task asks how they are written: content is what the texts carry, and the comparison’s grounds are form, structure and language. The missing half is the writing: both texts mention the cost, but one arrives as a figure in a report’s findings and the other as an image in a resident’s memory — and that difference, in the words and the structure, is what the ten analysis marks are for.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: content compared, writing unanalysed.
Must show the missing half: how the shared content is written differently, which the words and structure of each show.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Why must each difference in a comparison be explained by purpose, audience or context?
items.canonical_answer: The reason is that a difference without a reason is only an observation: two texts differ in a thousand ways, and the analysis is the selection of differences that mean something, which the purpose, audience or context supplies. A speech opens with a greeting because a hall must be found; an article opens with a headline because a reader must be caught — the reason is what makes the difference a decision rather than an accident, and the comparison exists to show decisions.
marking_guidance: Credit the reason: the explanation turns a difference into a decision the analysis can credit.
An answer that says differences are interesting has not answered the why.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Compare these two sentences about the same flooded bridge, written for the purpose — A is for officials, B is for friends: A: "Inspection of the northern abutment revealed structural compromise requiring closure." B: "Honestly, the bridge is worse than we thought — they’ve shut it." How does the change of audience work on the words?
items.canonical_answer: The change of audience works at every level. A’s passive ("was revealed" by implication) and Latinate vocabulary ("structural compromise") keep the officials at arm’s length and the blame diffuse, which suits a body that must act without alarming; B’s contraction and intensifier ("they’ve shut it", "worse than we thought") make it news between friends, and the passive disappears because a friend wants to know who shut the thing. The reader of A is invited to file; the reader of B is invited to gossip — the register, the grammar and the address all moved because the audience did.
marking_guidance: Must name the register change: Latinate and passive against contractions and directness.
Must trace the effect on each named reader: the official filed, the friend gossiped, because the words show who is addressed.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Text A devotes its first paragraph to the launch day’s crowd and its last to the funding pledge. Text B, from the same source, gives the pledge in its first line and never mentions the crowd. What do these details suggest about the two texts’ purposes?
items.canonical_answer: The details suggest different purposes at work on the same content: A’s crowd-first, pledge-last arrangement holds the funding back as a climax, which suggests a piece built to be enjoyed — a feature, where the story earns the news. B’s pledge-first, crowd-absent arrangement delivers the decision before anything else, which suggests a piece built to inform — a notice or a report, where the reader’s question is answered before it is asked. The same two facts, differently weighted, imply two purposes and two audiences: the reader who chose the story, and the reader who needs the decision.
marking_guidance: Must read the arrangement as evidence: held-back pledge implies a feature’s shape; pledge-first implies a notice’s.
Must say what the details suggest: purposes of entertaining-informing against informing, and the audiences each implies.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The tone of my response is urgent, while the source is calm." No words from either text appear. What is missing, and what is the rule?
items.canonical_answer: What is missing is the proof: a named tone is a claim, and the claim stands on the words that create it — the imperative verbs and short sentences that make urgency, the long balanced clauses that make calm. The rule is that a tone is shown in the words or it stays a guess: quote them, and the tone is analysis; assert it without them, and it is a claim the reader cannot check, worth little on any level table.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: the words that create the tone, missing from each text.
Must state the rule: tone is a claim proved by language, so the quotation is the tone’s evidence.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What does a strong comparative paragraph contain?
items.canonical_answer: A point about one text, the paired evidence from the other, and the explanation by purpose, audience or context — three moves, in every paragraph, repeated until the analysis ends. The connective is the visible sign of the pairing: whereas, similarly, both, and the paragraph that lacks one is describing, not comparing.
marking_guidance: Credit the three parts: point, paired evidence, explanation by purpose or audience.
The pairing in every paragraph is the feature that makes it comparative, so an answer without it has described a paragraph.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between comparing throughout and placing two commentaries side by side, and what is the test?
items.canonical_answer: Comparing throughout holds both texts in view in each paragraph, so every point is a relation; two separate commentaries side by side describe one text and then the other, and the reader must build every relation themselves, because no sentence refers across. The test is the cover-up: hide one column of the answer, and if the visible column still makes sense on its own, it was a description — a comparative sentence, with a connective at its hinge, loses its meaning when either text is removed.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: relations in every paragraph against descriptions laid side by side.
Must give the test: cover either column; a comparison stops making sense, a commentary does not.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: An answer has one paragraph on the source, then one on the response, then another on the source. What is the structural error, and what is the mechanical fix?
items.canonical_answer: The structural error is discussing each text in turn without ever referring across to the other: the paragraphs alternate, but no sentence holds both, so the comparison — the relation — never happens on the page. The mechanical fix is the connective: rewrite each paragraph to open with a whereas, similarly or both, so the point starts as a pair and the evidence has to arrive from both texts. The fix is mechanical because it can be checked by search: find the connectives, or find the paragraphs that need rebuilding.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: alternating paragraphs with no sentence referring across.
Must give the fix: the connective in every paragraph, checked mechanically, because the pairing then has to happen.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Read "The school that feeds itself" (Text 01 in this topic’s practice texts). The head learner has asked you to open the assembly by telling the school what its farm achieved this year. Write the opening of the speech, addressed to the students. Write your response in 150–200 words, re-using the text’s content in your own words. [10]
items.canonical_answer:
Good morning, assembly. I have a number for you: zero. That is what our kitchen spent on vegetables this year — nothing, nada — because the three hectares behind the sports field that used to be a lawn you were punished for mowing is now a farm that feeds this school.
You did this. The ag-science class planned the rotation. The egg co-operative banked thirty-one thousand dollars — I checked the ledger myself, and I would like to meet the learners who priced a rand of profit per carton and shake their hands. The maths class does its percentages on that same ledger, and the extension office quotes our pest blog, which I mention because I wrote the first rule of that blog: never let a good observation go unpublished.
There are challenges, and I will be honest: the borehole is ageing, we lost forty birds in one December week, and the horticulture post is empty. The award money waits for a plan, and the mayor’s promise waits with it.
So here is my ask: bring the plan with you. The farm taught you the weather does not read one. Neither does a school.
marking_guidance: Mark against both columns of the 10-mark table (reading /5, writing /5).

Reading (AO1): credit a subtle, assured grasp of the source’s meaning, context and audience, with its content drawn on perceptively — facts, viewpoint and people carried across in the learner’s own words.

Writing (AO2): credit assured, highly accurate writing whose vocabulary, style and structure suit the set form, audience and purpose, with the form’s conventions present and ideas developed throughout.
The model answer is the standard: the set form’s conventions, the source’s relevant content, and a fitted register, inside 150–200 words.
A Level 3 answer would keep the content but write more plainly, with some slips, its form conventions only partly present.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Compare the form, structure and language of Text 01 ("The school that feeds itself") with those of the directed response you wrote for ITEM-9093-1.4-P01 (the model response in this topic’s bank). Analyse how each text’s choices suit its audience and create meaning. [15]
items.canonical_answer:
The source is a news feature article for a regional readership, written in the third person with a wry institutional eye; my response is a speech to a school assembly, written in the first person by the school’s principal. Both texts carry the same content — the kitchen’s zero vegetable budget, the egg co-operative’s N$31,000, the retired horticulture teacher, the ageing borehole, the award money and the mayor’s promise — but the forms shape it differently, and the differences all have reasons in the audiences.
The openings show the contrast at once. The article opens with a headline and a standfirst — “KATIMA SOUTH SECONDARY SCHOOL DIDN’T SET OUT TO FEED ITSELF” — a paradox that teases a browsing reader into the story; my speech opens with “Good morning, assembly” and the figure “zero”, because a speech must find its hall before it can make its case, and a listening audience needs its news in the first minute. Whereas the article’s headline withholds, the greeting assures — two openings doing first contact for two different readers.
The voices differ accordingly. The article quotes Nakuta through reported speech and direct quotation — “we did not build a farm, we built a reason” — because a feature’s authority is borrowed from its sources; my speech is the authority itself, and its asides (“nothing, nada”) are the principal’s own voice, which no article could use. Both texts handle the learners’ pride similarly — Iipinge’s “the queue was the education” in the source; my “you did this” in the speech — but the source lets him speak for himself whereas the speech credits the hall directly, because a speaker praises to a hall’s face and a feature praises by quotation.
Structurally, the article alternates scene and quotation across paragraphs of descending length and ends on Iipinge carrying the egg crates — a closing image the reader leaves with; my speech ends on an imperative, “bring the plan with you”, because a speech’s close is its ask. items.prompt: Read "The night at the Otjiwarongo hall" (Text 09 in this topic’s practice texts). You are a critic who was in the audience. Write the review of the cultural evening, re-using what the musician’s account tells you happened. Write your response in 150–200 words, re-using the text’s content in your own words. [10]
items.canonical_answer:
Otjiwarongo Town Hall, Saturday: a cultural evening of uncommon nerve, and the reason to write about it is a sixteen-year-old with a guitar older than her mother.
Let the record show the evening’s best moment was not a prize-winner. The marimba band was tight; the drought poem earned its eleven minutes; the dance troupe danced eight seconds of jammed-tape silence without blinking, the oldest professionalism there is. But the hall made its sound only once — at the second verse of a hymn everyone present knew, when two hundred people decided at once not to be an audience.
The singer had walked to her chair after her name was said, tuned the guitar with the calm of someone lighting a candle, and opened her eyes-closed third song to the back wall, as her mother instructs. Her own first song will improve; the second did not need to.
The prize went to the poet, and rightly. The N$50 and a plate of food went to the girl, and I have watched professionals manage the silence between the name and the first note worse than she did.
Verdict: an evening with one future in it, and the future held the guitar.

items.canonical_answer:
My family is one of the numbers on the wall at the fuel station, and I mean that as a compliment. Our Water Ledger, week by week.
Every Friday my mother walks to the noticeboard and comes home with the town’s week in her head: the dam at 41 per cent, the schools down 44 per cent — fastest in town, and our head teacher says it like a score, which at our school it now is.
The repair brigade fixed our yard tap in March, within a week, and the woman who fixed it showed me the washer: fifty cents, and the town had pumped that leak for a year.
The tariff is what people argue about at the braai, so here is our bill: the first block got cheaper, the second more than doubled, and my mother calls the scheme the first thing the municipality has done that she can watch working.
The engineer says we bought time, not safety: nineteen months instead of eleven to critical. I think about that in the shower, on a timer now.
Two regions have come to look at our noticeboard. Three ideas and a noticeboard, the engineer calls it.

Councillors — good evening, and thank you for the two minutes, which I know cost more than my stall does.
I sell from the second stall from the gate, and I want to talk about the roof you are planning to demolish for the parking.
You have heard the market is a machine. It is. It runs on Saturdays, and on return customers — mine stay nine years, and I know their sizes, their daughters’ birthdays and their football, which is the market’s real inventory. And it runs on shade, the one thing I pay for that your plan cannot see.
The drawing puts the parking where the shelters are. You gain thirty cars and lose a machine paying rent on thirty stalls, on which your rates ride: the arithmetic is not close.
I ask for two things: keep the roof, and put a market seller on the committee that draws the next plan. We know where the shade falls at noon.
The gate opens at six. Come stand at the second stall, and watch the river come through it.
